name: Design a Stock Exchange
intent: Match buyers and sellers fairly and in strict order, in microseconds, with a record so complete that the whole day can be replayed and give exactly the same trades.
codeTitle: an order book with price-time priority
finalIntro: One buy order from a trader to a trade, and out to everyone watching the market.
prompt: Design the core of a stock exchange. Traders send buy and sell orders for thousands of symbols. The exchange matches them, tells both sides about the trade, and tells the whole market what the current prices are, fairly, fast, and without ever losing or reordering an order.
functional: Accept limit orders (a price limit) and market orders, and cancellations
Match each order against the other side of the book by price priority, then by time of arrival
Confirm trades to both traders, and publish trade and price information to everyone
Run risk checks before an order enters the book
Keep a complete, ordered audit trail of everything that happened
nonFunctional: Match an order in tens of microseconds, with very little variation between orders
Strict fairness: the same orders in the same order always give the same trades, and no one gets a faster path in
Never lose or reorder an acknowledged order, even if the machine running the match fails
Throughput of hundreds of thousands of orders per second for the busiest symbols
Recover from a machine failure in well under a second, with no trade lost or repeated
Everyone who watches the market sees the same updates in the same order

firstAttempt.text: A web application and a SQL database. An orders table holds the open orders. When an order arrives, a transaction looks up the best matching orders on the other side, updates them and inserts the trades, and commits. Many application servers run in parallel.
limits: A database transaction takes milliseconds, which is a thousand times too slow for a market
Several servers matching the same symbol at once fight over the same rows, and the outcome depends on who wins the race, so it is neither fair nor repeatable
Locking makes latency jump unpredictably, so some traders are consistently slower than others
Prices have to be polled from the database, so traders see different prices at different moments
One database is one point of failure for the whole market

nodes.label: Matching engines, one per group of symbols

steps.title: Match in a single thread, with the order book in memory
steps.problem: Database transactions and locks are far too slow, and concurrent matching makes the outcome depend on timing luck.
steps.fix: A matching engine keeps the order book of each symbol in memory: buy orders sorted from the highest price down, sell orders from the lowest price up, with each price level holding its orders in arrival order. A single thread takes one order at a time and matches it against the best opposite orders, so there are no locks and no races. Trades are written to a database afterwards, off the critical path.
steps.tradeoff: Each match takes microseconds, and the result depends only on the order of arrival, which is what fairness means. Throughput is limited to what one core can do, so the work is divided by symbol, and the state in memory must be protected against loss.

steps.title: Number every order in a sequencer, and journal it first
steps.problem: The engine's memory is lost in a crash, and orders arriving over several connections have no single agreed order.
steps.fix: All orders pass through a sequencer, which stamps each with the next sequence number and writes it to an append-only journal before anything else happens. The engine reads the journal in sequence order. The engine is a deterministic state machine: the same orders in the same order always produce exactly the same book and trades. So the journal, and nothing else, defines what happened, and any past moment can be reproduced by replaying it.
steps.tradeoff: There is one agreed order of events and a complete audit trail, and recovery is replay. The sequencer is on the critical path, so it must be extremely fast and itself replicated, and the engine may use nothing random and nothing that depends on the clock.

steps.title: Run hot standbys that read the same journal
steps.problem: If the engine's machine fails, the market stops, and rebuilding the book by replaying the whole day takes too long.
steps.fix: Standby engines run on other machines, in other racks, and consume the same journal in the same order. Because the engine is deterministic they always hold the identical book, a moment behind the primary. If the primary stops responding, a standby takes over from the last sequence number it processed. Orders are acknowledged only after they have been safely journaled on more than one machine.
steps.tradeoff: A failover takes a fraction of a second and loses nothing, because the standby has the same state. Writing to multiple machines before acknowledging adds a little latency to each order, and takeover must avoid two engines both thinking they are the primary.

steps.title: Split the symbols across engines
steps.problem: One engine thread cannot handle every symbol, but orders for different symbols never interact.
steps.fix: Assign each symbol, or a group of quiet symbols, to one engine, with its own sequencer, journal and standbys. Gateways route an order to the engine that owns its symbol. Very busy symbols get an engine of their own. Cross-symbol operations are rare and handled outside the matching path.
steps.tradeoff: Capacity grows by adding engines, and a problem with one symbol cannot affect the others. A single hot symbol is still limited by one engine, so it must be fast, and moving a symbol between engines needs a controlled hand-over.

steps.title: Check every order before it enters the book
steps.problem: A mistyped price or a runaway program can send orders that could do serious damage within seconds, and the matching engine has no time for slow checks.
steps.fix: A gateway authenticates each connection and runs pre-trade risk checks in memory before the order reaches the sequencer: the account's limits, the size and price of the order against the last price (to catch a mistyped 'fat finger'), and the rate of orders per second. Rejected orders never enter the journal. Each broker has its own gateway capacity, so a flood from one cannot slow the others.
steps.tradeoff: Dangerous orders stop at the door and the engine only sees valid ones. Checks add a few microseconds and must be kept simple, and limits need tuning so that they catch mistakes without rejecting real trading.

steps.title: Publish market data in order, to everyone at the same time
steps.problem: Thousands of firms need the same price changes at the same moment, and any unfairness in who hears first is a serious problem.
steps.fix: The engine emits an ordered stream of events: orders added, cancelled and traded, each with a sequence number. A feed publishes this stream to all subscribers at once, usually with multicast over a fast network, so everyone receives each update at the same time. Subscribers who miss a message notice the gap in sequence numbers and ask a recovery service for it, and new subscribers start from a snapshot of the book and then apply the updates that follow.
steps.tradeoff: Everyone sees the same updates in the same order at nearly the same time, and the engine does not slow down for slow readers. Multicast is unreliable, so gap detection and a recovery path are essential, and the feed and the engine are kept on separate machines.

failures.scenario: The primary matching engine's machine crashes in the middle of the trading day
failures.impact: The book in its memory is gone and no orders are being matched.
failures.answer: A hot standby, which has been applying the same journal, becomes the primary from the last sequence number and carries on within a fraction of a second. Orders that were journaled are never lost, and orders that were not acknowledged are resent by the traders' systems.

failures.scenario: A trader's system sends the same order twice after a timeout
failures.impact: Without protection, a trader buys twice as much as they meant to.
failures.answer: Every order carries a client order id, which is unique for that trader. The gateway or the engine rejects an id it has already seen, so the repeat is ignored and the trader is told about the original order.

failures.scenario: A firm's program goes wrong and sends a million orders in a second
failures.impact: The flood could fill the sequencer and delay everyone's orders.
failures.answer: The gateway rate-limits that firm's connection and stops the flow when it passes its limit, and an automatic kill switch cancels the firm's open orders. Because each firm has its own gateway capacity, the others do not notice.

failures.scenario: A subscriber misses part of the market data stream
failures.impact: Their picture of the order book is wrong, and they might trade on wrong prices.
failures.answer: Every message has a sequence number, so they notice the gap at once. They stop trusting their book, request the missing messages from the recovery service, or reload a snapshot and then apply newer updates.

alternatives.title: How matching is done

options.name: A database transaction per order
options.con: Milliseconds per order, and a lock fight between servers

options.name: A single-threaded in-memory engine
options.con: One core per symbol group, and state to protect

options.name: Several threads sharing one book with locks
options.con: Locks add delays and make the outcome depend on timing

alternatives.pick: A single-threaded in-memory engine per symbol group, with a journal for durability.

alternatives.title: How to share a price level between orders

options.name: Price-time priority (first in, first out)
options.pro: Simple, and rewards those who commit to a price first
options.con: A fast firm can always jump ahead by being first

options.name: Pro-rata
options.pro: Spreads a trade across everyone at the best price in proportion to their size
options.con: Rewards large orders, and invites inflating order sizes

alternatives.pick: Price-time priority is the common rule for shares. Pro-rata is more common in some interest-rate markets.

alternatives.title: How market data is delivered

options.name: Each subscriber polls a database
options.con: Different people see different prices at different times

options.name: TCP stream per subscriber
options.con: A slow subscriber holds back its own stream, and the engine sends once per subscriber, so someone is always first or last

options.name: Multicast with sequence numbers and recovery

alternatives.pick: Multicast with sequence numbers, snapshots and a recovery service.

alternatives.title: How the machine failure is survived

options.name: Restore from a backup and replay
options.con: Minutes of downtime during which there is no market

options.name: Hot standbys on the same journal
options.pro: Failover within a fraction of a second, losing nothing
options.con: Twice the machines, and the takeover logic has to be exactly right

alternatives.pick: Hot standbys fed from the replicated journal.

roles.label: Gateways
roles.description: The order gateway that authenticates and checks orders.

roles.label: Ordered streams
roles.description: The sequencer, journal and market data feed.

roles.label: Engines
roles.description: Matching engines, standbys and risk checks.

quiz.question: An exchange starts with several app servers that all match orders for the same symbol. Each runs a SQL transaction that finds the best opposite orders and updates them. Two sell orders reach different servers within the same microsecond. Traders complain that the same stream of orders sometimes gives different trades. What is the root problem and the fix?
options: Transactions are too slow, so move the order book into a Redis cache and keep the parallel servers doing the matching
Row-lock races decide who wins, so use one thread per symbol that matches an in-memory book in arrival order
The default isolation level is too weak, so switch to SERIALIZABLE and let the database abort and retry the losers
Servers see orders in different sequences, so route each trader to one fixed server with sticky sessions
quiz.explanation: Several writers on the same rows make the result depend on timing, so it is neither fair nor repeatable. A single thread over an in-memory book removes locks and races. SERIALIZABLE gives a safe result, but still a timing-dependent one, and costs milliseconds.

quiz.question: A matching engine writes every order to its own local journal and then acknowledges the trader. A standby copies the journal asynchronously. The primary machine dies and its disk is unrecoverable. The standby is missing a few orders that traders were told were accepted. Which change prevents this?
options: Take a snapshot of the order book every second and have the standby load the newest one when it takes over
Move the journal to faster NVMe storage so that the standby is never more than a microsecond behind
Ask traders to resend any order not shown as traded within one second of the acknowledgement
Acknowledge an order only after its journal entry is stored on at least two machines, accepting a little extra latency
quiz.explanation: An acknowledgement is a promise, so the entry must survive the loss of one machine before the promise is made. A one-second snapshot still loses up to a second of acknowledged orders. Faster disks shrink the gap but never close it, and resending puts the burden on traders.

quiz.question: A team lets the engine break ties between orders at the same price by reading the machine clock when each order is processed. After a failover, the standby, which replayed the same journal, reports different trades for the same orders. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The engine reads local time, so replicas disagree; use only journal sequence numbers, with no clock or random input
The standby replayed too slowly and skipped some orders, so give it more cores and let it replay with several threads at once
The two machines' clocks drifted apart, so synchronise them more tightly with PTP and keep reading the clock for tie-breaks
Journal entries were reordered on the way to the standby, so ship them over TCP and add a checksum and a length to each entry
quiz.explanation: Replay only gives identical results if the engine is a deterministic state machine, so any clock or random input breaks it. Tighter clock sync still leaves the result dependent on when each machine runs. The journal's sequence number already gives a single agreed order to use for ties.
